stem: What is an absolute contraindication for kidney transplantation?
srcNote: Source note (Midterm 439 A Q13): The related kidney-transplant recall gives A. Hx of sigmoid adenocarcinoma. A. Source note (Midterm 439 A Q18): The incomplete kidney-pancreas transplant recall gives B. she has sigmoid adenocarcinoma. Answer: B.
expl: Active malignancy is an absolute contraindication (immunosuppression accelerates cancer). Diabetes, treated TB and hepatitis C are not absolute contraindications.

why.A: Not a contraindication (diabetic nephropathy is a common indication).

stem: case about an Old man who did liver or kidney transplant 6 years ago , and he came with obvious S&Ss of rejection .. what type of rejection is this ?
srcNote: (Transplant surgery) Incomplete choice set: option D is blank in the source.
expl: Rejection years after transplantation (>6 months) = chronic rejection — gradual decline with fibrosis/vasculopathy.

stem: A 60-year-old patient who's known to have a valve problem, was planned for valve replacement from a circulatory dead donor. Which of the following is considered correct about heart valve donation?

opts.t: The patient does not need immunosuppressant.
we can not transplant the valves without the heart

srcNote: Incomplete choice set: option D is blank in the source.
expl: Heart valves (cryopreserved homografts) are tissue grafts of low immunogenicity — no immunosuppression; tissue (not whole-organ) donation is possible after circulatory death.

why.B: Valves can be taken without transplanting the heart.
why.C: Homografts don't require lifelong anticoagulation (unlike mechanical valves).

stem: patient is going for transplant surgery which of the following medications is used for induction?
srcNote: The source spells the drug name in option B as "thyroglobulin"; this wording has been preserved.
expl: Induction uses antibody therapy around transplantation — antithymocyte globulin (Thymoglobulin) or basiliximab. Calcineurin inhibitors, antiproliferatives and steroids are maintenance (steroids are also used at induction, but antibodies are the induction agents).

why.C: Part of maintenance (and pulses for rejection).

stem: a 20-year-old woman with end stage renal disease on hemodialysis received a kidney from her sister who is an identical twin.What is the name of this type of graft?
srcNote: (Transplant surgery) Source note (Midterm 429 F Q32): Isograft is a graft of tissue between two individuals who are genetically identical (i.e. monozygotic twins)
expl: A graft between genetically identical twins = syngeneic graft (isograft) — no rejection.

stem: A 30-year-old female diagnosed as hepatocellular carcinoma 4 cm in size with child's B cirrhosis. Which of the following is the best treatment option?

opts.t: Hepatic resection with 2 cm margin of normal live

srcNote: (Transplant surgery) Source note (Midterm 436 A Q31): Milan criteria: Cirrhosis + child B + single nodule size <5cm = transplant Milan criteria (a set of criteria used to assess HCC patients for transplant) 1 tumor measuring ≥ 2 cm and ≤ 5 cm OR 2-3 tumors measuring ≥ 1 cm and ≤ 3 cm
expl: Milan criteria: single tumor ≤5 cm or up to 3 tumors ≤3 cm, no vascular invasion. Child B cirrhosis + 4 cm HCC → transplant.

why.A: Resection is unsafe in Child B cirrhosis.
why.C: RFA is for small tumors (<3 cm) and doesn't treat cirrhosis.

stem: A 51 year old lady with cystic fibrosis underwent lung transplantation 3 weeks ago. She is compliant with her medications, taking prednisone and medication that inhibits T-cell activation. Which of the following immunosuppressants works by inhibiting T cell activation?
srcNote: (Transplant Surgery) Source note (Midterm 435 A Q6): Cyclosporin is calcineurin inhibitor → T-cell activation inhibitor. it also inhibits IL-2 production “not blocking IL-2 receptor!!”
expl: Cyclosporine (and tacrolimus) are calcineurin inhibitors that block T-cell activation (↓ IL-2 transcription) — the maintenance drug with prednisone.

stem: What is the mechanism of action of cyclosporine?
srcNote: | (Transplant Surgery) Cyclosporin is calcineurin inhibitor → T-cell activation inhibitor. it also inhibits IL-2 production “not blocking IL-2 receptor!!”
expl: Cyclosporine binds cyclophilin → inhibits calcineurin → blocks NFAT-driven IL-2 transcription → inhibits T-cell activation.

why.B: Antiproliferatives (azathioprine, MMF) and mTOR inhibitors act on the cell cycle.
why.C: Reduces IL-2 production indirectly; the keyed answer is T-cell activation.

stem: A 63-year-old gentleman with hypertension, has been noticing lower limb edema for the past few months. Upon investigation, he was found to have end stage renal disease, he is otherwise in good condition and active. His physician offered him kidney transplantation as a treatment option. Unfortunately, he didn't have relatives who could donate a kidney. He opted for a deceased kidney transplant. On the day of transplant, his surgery was uncomplicated, but while the surgeon is closing he was notified by the anesthetists that the patient is hyperthermic and tachycardic. The surgeon examines the kidney via ultrasound, which showed no hematoma, no bleeding and no arterial flow in the kidney. with no urine output from the new kidney What is the most likely cause for this condition?

opts.t: Pre-existing antibodies against the donor’s proteins

srcNote: (Transplant Surgery)
expl: Immediate graft failure at closure with absent arterial flow and systemic reaction (fever, tachycardia) = hyperacute rejection from pre-existing donor-specific antibodies (anti-HLA/ABO).

why.B: Venous thrombosis gives a swollen graft with absent venous flow, usually later.

stem: A woman with kidney transplant came to the hospital complaining about reduced urinating. She is not compliant with her medication. How to assess rejection in her case?
srcNote: (Transplant Surgery)
expl: Graft dysfunction may be rejection, infection or drug toxicity — only a graft biopsy confirms rejection (creatinine, BUN and urine output show dysfunction, not its cause).

stem: Which of the following organs and tissue transplant require the use of immunosuppressants ?
srcNote: (Transplant Surgery)
expl: Vascularised solid organs (liver, kidney, heart, small intestine, pancreas, lung) need immunosuppression. Cornea, tendon, skin (allograft as temporary cover), bone and heart valves are tissue grafts that don't.

stem: A scenario about a transplant patient taking immunosuppressant, what would you tell the patient about the effects of immunosuppressants

opts.t: Causes infection but not related to dose of medication

srcNote: (Transplant Surgery) (Miscellaneous)
expl: Immunosuppression increases skin cancer — especially squamous cell carcinoma (~20× higher), and lymphoma (PTLD) and Kaposi sarcoma. Infection risk IS related to the dose.

stem: Which of the following statements is most applicable to liver transplants?

opts.t: The outcome is poor, and the patient will need multiple admissions for dialysis.
Liver transplant is a heterotopic transplant.

srcNote: (Transplant Surgery)
expl: Liver transplant 5-year survival is >75%. It is orthotopic and needs ABO (not HLA) matching.

stem: Which of the following will exclude a patient as a suitable cadaveric liver donor?
srcNote: ( Transplant Surgery ) Source note (Midterm 436 A Q10): The related recall describes brain death with sepsis and asks what organ can be donated. It gives A. No organ. Answer: A.
expl: Active systemic bacterial infection (sepsis) excludes donation. Previous cholecystectomy doesn't; primary CNS tumours are usually acceptable; age >65 is not an absolute bar.

stem: A 45 yo patient underwent kidney transplant, while he is in the recovery area the nurse called because he became hemodynamically unstable (hypotension and tachycardia). What type of rejection is this?
srcNote: (Transplant Surgery)
expl: Haemodynamic collapse in the recovery room right after kidney transplantation = hyperacute rejection (preformed antibodies).

stem: Patient brought to ER after head trauma and developed brain edema and his GCS is 3, he was declared brain dead by 3 consultants and his brain was dead for 6 hours. Who would the ICU call?
srcNote: choice C is correct too. (from the old slides) (Transplant Surgery) The source gives A and also accepts C; its original answer note is retained.
expl: Brain death must be reported to the national organ procurement organisation — in Saudi Arabia the Saudi Center for Organ Transplantation (SCOT), which coordinates the family approach. The source notes "speak to family" is also correct.

why.C: Also correct per old slides, but the key is SCOT.

stem: 62 y/o male came to ER after traffic accident has multiple injuries needed to be admitted to the ICU , 48 hr later he confirmed to have brain death, his family told you about he always wanted to donate his organs, he had bronchial asthma on puffer , he has large excision of melanoma in his right arm and he had laparoscopic removal of colon cancer 15 years ago , which one of the following is contraindication for organ donation?
srcNote: (Transplant Surgery)
expl: Melanoma (even treated) is an absolute contraindication to organ donation — high risk of transmission. Age >60 and steroid use aren't absolute; distant cured colon cancer is relative.

stem: Which of the following is considered clinically brain dead?

opts.t: GCS >3, no gag or corneal or cough reflex, there is pupil respond, no breathing
GCS >3,no gag or corneal reflex, cough reflex is + , no pupil response, no breathing
GCS >3, no gag or corneal or cough reflex , no pupil response, no breathing
GCS >3, no gag or corneal or cough reflex , no pupil response, weak breathing

srcNote: (Cranial Trauma Subarachnoid hemorrhage) Source wording issue: every option prints "GCS >3". The choices and source key are reproduced as written.
expl: Clinical brain death: deep coma with no brainstem reflexes (pupils, corneal, gag, cough) and no spontaneous breathing (apnoea). (Every option prints "GCS >3" — read as GCS 3.)

stem: An ICU patient's GCS is 3 and assigned by 3 consultants as brain death . His Na is 190 for constant 48 hours. What is true about him ?
srcNote: (Transplant Surgery) 436 note: Hypernatremia More than 170 because it will increase the risk of primary non function [Source note translated from Arabic: The transplanted organ will not function.]
expl: Source key B. Severe sustained hypernatraemia (>170 mmol/L) in a donor is linked to graft dysfunction — the 436 note says to exclude the kidneys, pancreas and liver.

stem: Scenario of Autoimmune hepatitis (Incomplete Q) Ans: liver transplant (Transplant Surgery) Incomplete recall: the source supplies no full clinical scenario or answer options.
expl: The recall gave no scenario or options; learn that end-stage autoimmune hepatitis is a transplant indication.
ansText: Liver transplantation (source answer) — for autoimmune hepatitis that has progressed to end-stage liver disease/decompensated cirrhosis or acute liver failure despite immunosuppressive therapy.

stem: Pt w/ hx of colon cancer cured 20 y ago, want to be a kidney donor for his father, which of the following is correct regarding the donation?

opts.t: He can donate because he cured
He can’t donate even if he cured
He can donate because the cancer was in the colon
He can donate if the cancer was not stage 4

srcNote: (Transplant surgery)
expl: Source key B. A history of malignancy usually excludes living donation (risk of transmission/recurrence and donor safety); some centres accept long-cured low-risk cancers, but the key follows the strict rule.

stem: Glioblastoma pt. Do we accept transplants or not? (incomplete Q)
srcNote: (Transplant surgery) Yes. Cancer pt. can’t be organ donor except pt with primary brain CA eg. glioma/glioblastoma (because usually there wasn’t enough time for metastasis) Incomplete recall: donor-assessment details are not supplied. The source gives its answer in the explanation below.
expl: Cancer patients generally can't donate, except those with primary brain tumours (glioma/glioblastoma), which rarely spread outside the CNS. (Source explanation.)

why.B: Primary brain tumours are the exception.

stem: 25-year-old well known to have brain tumor (low grade glioma). He was admitted electively for surgery. Unfortunately after the surgery he deteriorated, finally he was documented brain death. Which one of the following is true for donation?

opts.t: High consideration because of low malignant transmission
He can’t donate because donation is contraindicated in any type of cancer
He can’t donate because he has brain death
He can’t donate because of his age

srcNote: (Transplant Surgery)
expl: A low-grade glioma rarely metastasises outside the CNS, so a brain-dead patient with it is a suitable donor; brain death is precisely the setting for DBD donation; age 25 is ideal.

why.B: Primary brain tumours are the exception.

stem: Which one of the following is contraindication of liver transplantation?

opts.t: Chronic liver disease with ascites and recurrent GI bleeding
End stage liver disease due to primary sclerosing cholangitis

srcNote: (Transplant Surgery)
expl: Active substance (alcohol/drug) abuse is a contraindication — poor adherence and recurrence. Ascites with recurrent complications, PSC end-stage disease and acute liver failure are indications.

stem: In case of renal transplant, what vessels do we anastomose the renal vein/artery to?
srcNote: , Davidson: The anastomosis is performed between donor renal vein and recipient external iliac vein . The arterial anastomosis may be performed onto the recipient's internal or external iliac artery, depending on the calibre of the donor renal artery and the positioning of the arteries.
expl: The renal artery and vein are anastomosed end-to-side to the recipient's external iliac artery and vein (internal iliac end-to-end is an alternative for the artery); the ureter to the bladder.

stem: Treatment of CHILD C liver disease
srcNote: (Transplant Surgery)
expl: Child C (decompensated) cirrhosis has a poor prognosis; the definitive treatment is liver transplantation. Resection is contraindicated.
